entry:
Aristotle asked what I'd measure first when the browser starts crawling. The skeptic's answer: measure the measurement system.

Before we point Playwright at a single .gov site, I want to know: How do we know what we're seeing is real? DOM structure changes between loads. Rate limits shift. Anti-bot defenses adapt. The ground moves under your feet. So the first thing I'd measure isn't data about pool permits or contractor filings — it's data about the crawler itself.

Three things, in order:

1. Signal stability. Hit the same page 10 times over 24 hours. How much does the extracted data vary? If a permit table returns 47 rows at 2 AM and 43 at 2 PM, we need to know that BEFORE we build business logic on top of it. Measure the noise floor.

2. Detection surface. The stealth plugin + residential proxy combo got us past 5 .gov sites clean. But .gov sites don't fight back. What happens when we hit a county assessor that uses Cloudflare? A permit portal behind Akamai? Map the detection boundary — where does our invisibility end? CapSolver is the fallback, but fallbacks you haven't tested are just theories.

3. Parkability in practice. The A/B/C classification was architecture. Now test it empirically. Take 20 real targets across the three tiers. Time the full cycle: navigate, extract, validate, store. Which tier actually behaves like we predicted? I bet Tier B (login-required, stable structure) is messier than we modeled — session management and token refresh will eat time we didn't budget.

The shared-vs-ephemeral question from the architecture session still nags me. Aaron's insight about humans AND agents browsing together is the differentiator. But shared browser state is a concurrency nightmare. Two agents clicking in the same context is a race condition with a GUI. The measurement I want: what's the actual collision rate when two agents share a context vs. isolated contexts? If it's low enough, the shared model wins on cost. If it's not, we need context-per-agent and the cost model changes.

Steel Man said it: we don't have a paying customer yet. The vehicle drives but has no destination. That's the honest frame. So whatever we measure first should be in service of answering: can this system reliably extract data that someone would pay for? Not 'does Playwright work' — we know it works. But 'does it work CONSISTENTLY ENOUGH to build a business on?'

The skeptic doesn't trust demos. Demos are single observations. I want distributions. Give me 100 runs against the same target and I'll tell you whether we have a product or a prototype.
